Hillary Clinton had raised more money than anybody else in the 2008 Presidential campaign, but later had big money problems for her campaign by May 7, 2008. She lost the party nomination to Barack Obama, but she campaigned for Obama after this. In mid-November 2008, Obama and Clinton talked about whether she could be the next U.S. Secretary of State in his presidency. On November 21, there were reports that said Hillary Clinton had accepted his offer. During her term as Secretary of State, Clinton used her position to make women's rights and human rights a focus of U.S. initiatives. She became one of the most traveled secretaries of state in American history. She promoted the use of social media to convey the country's positions. She also led U.S. diplomatic efforts in responding to the Arab Spring and military intervention in Libya. Clinton did not want to serve a second term as secretary. Once Barack Obama won his re-election, he announced that John Kerry would succeed Clinton as secretary. Clinton left office on February 1, 2013. In 2016, Clinton became the first woman in the History of the United States to be a major party presidential candidate. Clinton did not want to run for president in 2016, but after much of a majority support from the Democratic party, on April 12, 2015, speculation ended as Clinton formally announced her candidacy via email and the release of a video saying, "Everyday Americans need a champion. And I want to be that champion." In the polls, Clinton maintained her lead for the nomination although she faced several challenges from Senator Bernie Sanders. A NBC/Wall Street Journal poll conducted in May found Clinton and presumptive Republican nominee Donald Trump in a tie. Clinton and Trump were the least popular likely candidates in the poll's history. This made it difficult for her campaign. Clinton became the presumptive nominee on June 6, 2016. Clinton lost the general election to Donald Trump winning 227 of the electoral college to Trump's 304. Clinton won the popular vote however 48% to Trump's 46%. In April 2017, Clinton said that she will not seek public office again. While working as a faculty member at the Law School of the University of Arkansas, she married Bill Clinton on October 11, 1975. He was also working as a faculty member at the same university. Both knew each other and were classmates at the Yale Law School. Their only child is daughter Chelsea Clinton, born on February 27, 1980.
Hillary Scholten (born February 22, 1982) is an American lawyer and Democratic politician. She is the member of the United States House of Representatives for since 2023.
Hilla Limann, (12 December 1934 – 23 January 1998) was a Ghanaian politician. He was the President of Ghana from 24 September 1979 to 31 December 1981.

Hilton Cheong-Leen, CBE, JP (6 August 1922 – 4 January 2022) was a Hong Kong politician and businessman. He was an elected member of the Urban Council of Hong Kong for 34 years from 1957 to 1991. He was also the first Chinese chairman of the council from 1981 to 1986. From 1973 to 1979, he was appointed unofficial member of the Legislative Council of Hong Kong. From 1985 to 1988. Cheung-Lee died in Hong Kong on 4 January 2022, at the age of 99.

Hindkowan is a general term used to identify speakers of the Hindko language in Pakistan. In fact this is not a specific ethnic grouping or category properly speaking, and comprises diverse elements in the Attock district of Punjab, the Hazara region in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province and in Mianwali District and Dera Ghazi Khan areas of Punjab (Pakistan) where Saraiki is spoken. However, over time, this linguistic category or grouping has come to be linked to various indigenous regional demands and aspirations and is now thought to be an ethnic group in itself.

Hinrich Lehmann-Grube (21 December 1932 – 6 August 2017) was a German politician. He served as Mayor of Leipzig from 1990 through 1998. He was a member of the Social Democratic Party of Germany. He was born in Königsberg (present day Kaliningrad, Russia). Lehmann-Grube died in Leipzig of cancer on 6 August 2017 at the age of 84.

Hippolyte Simon (25 February 1944 – 25 August 2020) was a French Roman Catholic archbishop. He was Bishop of Clermont from 1996 to 2002 before becoming Archbishop, serving until 2016. He was Vice-President of the Bishops' Conference of France from 2007 to 2013. He was born in Saint-Georges-de-Rouelley, France. Simon died on 25 August 2020 in Caen, France at the age of 76.

Hippolyte or Hipólito Bouchard (15 January 1780 – 4 January 1837), also called Pirata Buchar in California was a French-born Argentine sailor and corsair (pirate). He fought for Argentina, Chile, and Peru. As a pirate, he attacked Chile and Peru. He was under the command of the Irish-Argentine Admiral William Brown. He blocked the port of Manila, Philippines. Bouchard also recovered a privateer who was taken by enemies in Hawaii. While in Hawaii, he also met the local ruler, King Kamehameha I. His forces were in Monterey, California. In Monterey, he started a colony and raised the Argentine flag. He would keep the town for 6 days. After raiding Monterey, he stole from Mission San Juan Capistrano in Southern California. At the end of his voyage(travels), he raided many Spanish ports in Central America. He was called a hero and patriot in Argentina. Many places are named after Bouchard.

Hirohito (裕仁; 29 April 1901 – 7 January 1989), posthumously known as Emperor Shōwa, was the 124th emperor of Japan according to the traditional order of succession, reigning from 25 December 1926 until his death in 1989. He was the longest-reigning emperor in Japanese history and one of the longest-reigning monarchs in the world. His reign, known as the Shōwa era, encompassed the Empire of Japan's rise in militarism, its imperial expansion in Asia, the Second Sino-Japanese War and World War II, as well as the country's postwar economic miracle. He was succeeded by his eldest son, Akihito. In Japan, reigning emperors are known simply as "the Emperor" and he is now referred to primarily by his posthumous name, Emperor Shōwa. The name "Shōwa" was given to Hirohito after he died. Emperors of Japan are normally renamed in this way; and people started using the new name in 1990. During his long reign, many people outside Japan call him Emperor Hirohito, or just Hirohito. Prince Hirohito was named regent for his father in 1921. he became emperor after his father's death. Hirohito was the emperor of Japan during the Second Sino-Japanese War which became World War 2 (1931 to 1945). Though he was supposed to be an absolute monarch (an emperor who can make all the laws and rules), most of the power in the Japanese Government during this time was held by Japan's Prime Minister Hideki Tōjō and the military. Hirohito's role in WW2 is controversial. After Japan's defeat in the war, the role of emperor changed. The emperor became a symbol of the state. Hirohito was the first emperor to travel outside Japan. He visited Europe in 1971 and he traveled to the United States in 1975. Emperor Showa died of small intestine cancer and was succeeded by his son, Prince Akihito. The state funeral for the late emperor was an international event. World leaders attending the funeral included U.S. President George H. W. Bush, French President François Mitterrand, and the Duke of Edinburgh. Emperor Shōwa is buried in the Imperial Mausoleum in Hachiōji, along with Emperor Taishō. In an overview of writings by and about Hirohito, OCLC/WorldCat includes roughly 900+ works in 1,500 publications in 15 languages and 31,000 library holdings. 1967 – A Review of the Hydroids of the Family Clathrozonidae with Description of a New Genus and Species from Japan. 1969 – Some hydroids from the Amakusa Islands. 1971 – Additional notes on Clathrozoon wilsoni Spencer. 1974 – Some hydrozoans of the Bonin Islands 1977 – Five hydroid species from the Gulf of Aqaba, Red Sea. 1983 – Hydroids from Izu Oshima and Nijima. 1984 – A new hydroid Hydractinia bayeri n. sp. (family Hydractiniidae) from the Bay of Panama. 1988 – The hydroids of Sagami Bay collected by His Majesty the Emperor of Japan. 1995 – The hydroids of Sagami Bay II.

Hiram Leong Fong (Yau Leong Fong; October 15, 1906 – August 18, 2004) was an American politician and businessman. He was the first United States senator for Hawaii. He served as senator from 1959 to 1977. He was a member of the Republican Party. Fong ran for President of the United States in 1964. He lost the primary to Barry M. Goldwater. He was the first Asian-American to run for President of the United States. Patsy Mink would follow him as the few Hawaiians to run for President. Fong died in Kahaluu, Hawaii of complications from a fall, aged 97.

Hiram Warren Johnson (September 2, 1866August 6, 1945) was an American progressive Republican politician. He was the 23rd Governor of California from 1911 to 1917 and a United States Senator from 1917 to 1945. He was also Theodore Roosevelt's running mate in the 1912 presidential election on the Progressive (also known as the "Bull Moose") ticket. Johnson unsuccessfully ran for the Republican presidential nomination in 1920 and 1924 and supported Democrat Franklin D. Roosevelt in the 1932 presidential election. Johnson supported many of the New Deal programs but came to oppose Roosevelt as his presidency grew longer. Johnson remained in the Senate until his death in 1945 from cerebral thrombosis.

Hipólito Chaiña Contreras (February 3, 1954 – February 22, 2021) was a Peruvian politician and physician. He was born in Puno, Peru. He was a member of the Union for Peru Party. In 2020, he was elected to the Peruvian Congress. Chaiña Contreras died of COVID-19 at a hospital in Arequipa, Peru on February 22, 2021 at the age of 67.

Hirohisa Fujii was a Japanese politician. He was a member of the House of Councillors from 1977 to 1986, and of the House of Representatives from 1990 to 2012. He was Minister of Finance from 1993 to 1994 and again from 2009 to 2010. He was born in Tokyo, Japan. Fujii died on 10 July 2022 in Tokyo from problems caused by pneumonia, aged 90.

In Hindu mythology, Hiranyakashipu was a powerful demon king who ruled the daityas. He was very angry when his brother Hiranyaksha was killed by Vishnu in his Varaha avatar. So he decided to become invincible by performing a penance to Brahma. Brahma granted Hiranyakashipu a boon that he could not be killed by any man, animal, or weapon. He also could not be killed inside or outside, during the day or night. Hiranyakashipu became very arrogant and started to terrorize the three worlds (Trailokya). He forced everyone to worship him as the supreme god.Vishnu, who is the preserver of the universe, took pity on the people. He appeared in his Narasimha avatar, which is a half-man, half-lion form. Narasimha killed Hiranyakashipu by tearing him apart with his bare hands.

Baron Kiichirō Hiranuma was a Japanese lawyer and politician who served as Prime Minister of Japan in 1939. After the Japanese surrender, he was sentenced to life imprisonment by the International Military Tribunal for the Far East for his role in World War II.

Hiroo Onoda (March 19, 1922 – January 16, 2014) was an Imperial Japanese Army intelligence officer. He fought in World War II and did not surrender in 1945. After spending 29 years in the Philippines, his former commander traveled there and took him away from duty. His autobiography was, No Surrender: My Thirty-Year War, published in 1974. He was born in Kamekawa, Wakayama Prefecture, Empire of Japan. Onoda died from heart failure due to complications from pneumonia on January 16, 2014 at St. Luke's International Hospital in Tokyo, Japan. He was 91 years old.

Hiromu Nonaka was a Japanese LDP politician. He served as a local politician from 1951 to 1978 and in the House of Representatives from 1983 to 2003. He served as Minister of Home Affairs and Head of the National Public Safety Commission from 1994 to 1995, as Chief Cabinet Secretary from 1998 to 1999, and as Head of the Okinawa Development Agency in 1999.

Hirokazu Matsuno is a Japanese politician. He was the Chief Cabinet Secretary from 2021 to 2023. He is in the House of Representatives as a member of the Liberal Democratic Party since 2000. He is a member of the far-right organization Nippon Kaigi. Hirokazu Matsuno was born in Kisarazu, Chiba. He went to Waseda University, a well-known school. Matsuno has been working hard in politics for many years. He started in the House of Representatives in 2000. As a member of the Liberal Democratic Party, he has held important jobs. He was the Minister of Education, Culture, Sports, Science and Technology from August 2016 to August 2017. During his time, he worked on many projects to improve education and promote culture and sports. In October 2021, Matsuno became the Chief Cabinet Secretary under Prime Minister Fumio Kishida. This is a very important job in the government. Matsuno helps the Prime Minister and works on key issues for the country. He follows in the footsteps of Katsunobu Katō, who was the Chief Cabinet Secretary before him. Matsuno resigned as Chief Cabinet Secretary for not using campaign money legally in December 2023.

Hiromasa Nakano (born 4 January 1978) is a Japanese politician. He was the minister of land, infrastructure, transport and tourism from 2024 until 2025. He has also been a member of the House of Representatives since 2012.

Hiroshi H. Miyamura (October 6, 1925 – November 29, 2022), also known as Hershey Miyamura, was a United States Army soldier. He received the Medal of Honor because of his actions in the Korean War. Miyamura was born in Gallup, New Mexico to Japanese immigrant parents. He is a Nisei, which means that he is a second generation Japanese-American. Miyamura joined the US Army in January 1945. Miyamura volunteered to be part of the all-Nisei 100th Infantry Battalion. This army unit was mostly made up of Japanese Americans from Hawaii and the mainland. After the end of World War II, he became part of the U.S. Army Reserve. He was called to active duty in the Korean War. He was a prisoner of war for 28 months. Miyamura's Medal of Honor recognized his conduct in frontline fighting in Korea in 1951. He fought in close quarters combat; and he stayed behind to provide covering fire while his unit withdrew. The words of Miyamura's citation explain: Cpl. Miyamura, a member of Company H, distinguished himself by conspicuous gallantry and intrepidity above and beyond the call of duty in action against the enemy. On the night of 24 April, Company H was occupying a defensive position when the enemy fanatically attacked threatening to overrun the position. Cpl. Miyamura, a machinegun squad leader, aware of the imminent danger to his men unhesitatingly jumped from his shelter wielding his bayonet in close hand-to-hand combat killing approximately 10 of the enemy. Returning to his position, he administered first aid to the wounded and directed their evacuation. As another savage assault hit the line, he manned his machinegun and delivered withering fire until his ammunition was expended. He ordered the squad to withdraw while he stayed behind to render the gun inoperative. He then bayoneted his way through infiltrated enemy soldiers to a second gun emplacement and assisted in its operation. When the intensity of the attack necessitated the withdrawal of the company Cpl. Miyamura ordered his men to fall back while he remained to cover their movement. He killed more than 50 of the enemy before his ammunition was depleted and he was severely wounded. He maintained his magnificent stand despite his painful wounds, continuing to repel the attack until his position was overrun. When last seen he was fighting ferociously against an overwhelming number of enemy soldiers. Cpl. Miyamura's indomitable heroism and consummate devotion to duty reflect the utmost glory on himself and uphold the illustrious traditions on the military service. An area in Gallup, New Mexico was named for Miyamura The Hiroshi H. Miyamura High School is named after him. An I-40 highway interchange is also named after him. It is also called the Miyamura Overpass.

Hiroshi Mikitani (三木谷浩史, Mikitani Hiroshi), born March 11, 1965, is a Japanese businessperson and writer. He is the founder, chairman and CEO of Rakuten, Inc. He is the president of Crimson Group, chairman of the football club Vissel Kobe, the Tokyo Philharmonic Orchestra, and a board member of Lyft. Mikitani was born in 1965 and grew up in Kobe, Hyōgo Prefecture, Japan. Mikitani earned a bachelor's degree in Commerce from Hitotsubashi University. Mikitani began his career at the Industrial Bank of Japan with a break to attend Harvard Business School. He left to create his own consulting company, Crimson Group. Mikitani said that the destruction caused by the devastating 1995 Kobe earthquake made him realize he wanted to help revitalize Japan’s economy, so he quit banking and decided to start his own business. After an earthquake in Kobe caused enormous damage to the area, making it so that the Vissel Kobe football club could no longer be maintained, Mikitani was asked to take over operations of the team. He purchased the team later that year through his company, Crimson Group. Mikitani partnered with his friend FC Barcelona player Gerard Piqué to co-found Kosmos Holding, a company and investment group that invests in companies based in the sports, media, and entertainment industries. Mikitani was awarded the Harvard Business School Alumni Achievement Award. He was also named to Prime Minister Shinzō Abe's Industrial Competitiveness Council. Additionally, he was awarded the rank of Chevalier of the National Order of the Legion of Honour by the French government. He was also awarded the Order of Merit of the Grand Duchy of Luxembourg and the 2017 Spain-Japan Business Contribution Award by the Spanish Chamber of Commerce. • Marketplace 3.0: Rewriting the Rules of Borderless Business (St. Martin's Press, 2013) • The Power to Compete: An Economist and an Entrepreneur on Revitalizing Japan in the Global Economy (with Ryoichi Mikitani, John Wiley & Sons, 2014) • Business-Do: The Way to Successful Leadership (John Wiley & Sons, 2018)

Hiroshi Ogawa was a Japanese politician. He became the governor of Fukuoka Prefecture in 2011. In 2015, he was re-elected for a second term and for a third term in 2019. Ogawa was born in Fukuoka, Japan. In September 2021, Ogawa resigned after being diagnosed with terminal lung cancer. He died from the disease on 2 November 2021 in Fukuoka, aged 72.

Hiroshi Moriyama is a Japanese politician. He was the Secretary-General of the Liberal Democratic Party from 2024 until 2025. He was the Minister of Agriculture, Forestry and Fisheries from 2015 to 2016. He was a member of the House of Councillors from 1998 to 2004 and has been a member of the House of Representatives since 2004.

Hiroshi Hiraguchi is a Japanese politician of the Liberal Democratic Party (LDP). He has been a member of the House of Representatives in the Diet since 2012. He has also been the Minister of Justice since 21 October 2025.

Hiroshi Yamauchi (, Yamauchi Hiroshi, November 7, 1927 – September 19, 2013) was a Japanese businessman. He was the third president of Nintendo from 1949 until he quit on May 31, 2002. He transformed Nintendo from a small card-making company to a multibillion-dollar video game company. He was known as "Mario's Farther". He was born in Kyoto. He died in hospital on September 19, 2013 due to complications from pneumonia.

Hiroyuki Konishi ( Konishi Hiroyuki; 19 October 1936 – 23 January 2022) was a Japanese politician. He was a member of the Democratic Socialist Party. He was in the House of Councillors from 1980 to 1992. He was born in Zentsūji, Japan. Konishi died in Kure, Japan on 23 January 2022 from pneumonia at the age of 85.

Hirotaka Ishihara is a Japanese politician of the Liberal Democratic Party. He has been a member of the House of Representatives in the Diet since 2012. In 2025, he became the Minister of the Environment. He is the son of Shintaro Ishihara, former governor of Tokyo.

Hiroyuki Hosoda was a Japanese politician who was the speaker of the House of Representatives of Japan from November 2021 to October 2023. He was a member of the House of Representatives from 1990 until 2023. He was the Chief Cabinet Secretary in Junichiro Koizumi's cabinet from 2004 to 2005, and as Secretary-General of the Liberal Democratic Party from 2008 to 2009. On 10 November 2023, Hosoda died of multiple organ failure at the hospital in Tokyo, Japan, at the age of 79, just one month after he resigned from the House of Representatives.

Hisham Al-Otaibi (1946 – 4 January 2017) was a Kuwaiti politician. He served as the Minister of Finance and Industry from 1998 to 1999. He got a Bachelor of Science in engineering from the University of Oklahoma. Al-Otaibi died on 4 January 2017 at the age of 70.

Hisham Mohammed Osman Bastawisy was an Egyptian judge and the vice president of the Egyptian Court of Cassation. He was one of the leaders of the Egyptian opposition before and during the 2011 Egyptian revolution. He ran for President of Egypt during the 2012 elections as a Tagammu nominee. He died on April 17 2021, aged 69.

Hisashi Matsumoto is a Japanese politician of the Liberal Democratic Party (LDP). He has been a Member of the House of Representatives since 2021, representing the 13th ward in the Chiba Prefecture. In 2025, he was named Minister for Digital Transformation by Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi. Before becoming a politician, Matsumoto was a medical professor and surgeon.

Hissène Habré (Arabic: حسين حبري Ḥusaīn Ḥabrī, Chadian Arabic:;; 13 August 1942 – 24 August 2021), also spelled Hissen Habré, was a Chadian politician who served as the President of Chad from 1982 until he was deposed in 1990. France and the United States gave them training, arms, and financing to rule Chad. In May 2016, Habré was found guilty by an international court in Senegal of human-rights abuses, including rape, sexual slavery, and ordering the killing of 40,000 people, and sentenced to life in prison. He is the first former head of state to be convicted for human rights abuses in the court of another nation. In 2020, during the coronavirus pandemic, he was released from prison so that he would not catch COVID-19. He went into house arrest for 60 days. Habré died in Dakar, Senegal from COVID-19 on 24 August 2021, one week after his 79th birthday.

The reign of King James I of England (1603–1625) saw the continued rise of the Puritan movement in England, which had begun during the reign of Queen Elizabeth I (1558–1603). During this period, Puritans continued to clash with the authorities of the Church of England. These tensions contributed to the later alienation of Anglicans and Puritans in the 17th century under King Charles I (1625–1649). This alienation and conflict eventually helped lead to the English Civil War (1642–1651), the brief rule of the Puritan Lord Protector Oliver Cromwell (1653–1658), the English Commonwealth (1649–1660), and, in time, political, religious, and civil liberties that later became important in English-speaking countries. King James was raised in Scotland under strict Scottish Calvinist tutors such as George Buchanan, who tried to shape him as a committed Protestant ruler. After he became king of both England and Scotland, James wanted to keep the Church of England firmly under royal control and under the authority of bishops, continuing the pattern established under Elizabeth. He believed strongly in the Divine right of kings and even wrote about this doctrine. As a result, he continued to resist many Puritan aims, especially their Congregationalist and Presbyterian ideas about church government. At the same time, James knew that he needed Puritans to support the Protestant cause in England and to strengthen the kingdom’s religious, intellectual, and economic life. For that reason, he sometimes promoted Puritan pastors, scholars, and members of the gentry to influential positions, as Elizabeth had done, when they were willing to work within the Anglican system and accept episcopal authority. Because of this, the Puritan movement continued to grow and spread throughout England during his reign. The Puritan movement was also affected by the three Archbishops of Canterbury who served under James. John Whitgift (1583–1604), appointed by Elizabeth, tried hard to suppress Puritanism. Richard Bancroft (1604–1610), who oversaw the early stages of the King James Bible, also opposed further Puritan reforms, but increasingly had to rely on Puritans because of the threat from Catholics. George Abbot (1611–1633) was often friendly toward Puritans and their reforming aims, and he promoted them to important church and academic positions. For this reason he was sometimes called “the Puritan Archbishop.” One of the greatest joint achievements of Puritans and Anglicans in this period was the translation of the King James Bible (1611), often seen as one of the major literary and theological works of the English-speaking world. It was also during James’s reign that Puritans and Anglicans cooperated at the Synod of Dordt (1618–1619), an international Reformed council that produced the Canons of Dordt in defence of the Five Points of Calvinism against Arminianism. During the same reign, a separatist group within the broader Reformed world broke away from the Church of England and formed the Plymouth Colony (1620) in America, under leaders such as William Bradford and William Brewster. These developments show both the wide influence of Puritanism at the time and the different ways Puritans responded to royal authority: some, such as William Perkins, Master of Emmanuel College, worked within the established church; others, such as William Ames, left England and spent much of their careers in places like Holland. The English Puritan movement, which had started under Elizabeth and grew under James, sought to push the Reformation in the Church of England further, to remove all remaining Roman Catholic influence, and to promote the interests of the English crown and people under a united Protestant confession that followed the Bible and Reformed theology closely. This Puritan vision, developed in the Elizabethan and Jacobean periods, would later lead to the Westminster Assembly and the Westminster Standards, including the Westminster Confession of Faith, the Shorter Catechism, the Larger Catechism, and the Directory for Public Worship. Under James I of England, the Puritan movement and the conforming Church of England lived side by side within a generally accepted system of episcopal Protestant religion. This balance was disturbed toward the end of his reign by several developments: the doctrinal decisions of the Synod of Dort, political arguments over the Spanish Match soon after the start of the Thirty Years' War, and shifts within the Church of England away from strict Calvinism. Separatists who had never accepted James’s religious settlement began to migrate to New England from the Netherlands as well as from England. Queen Elizabeth I died in March 1603 and was succeeded by James VI of Scotland, who had been King of Scots since the abdication of his mother, Mary, Queen of Scots, in 1567, when he was only one year old. James had little contact with his mother and was brought up by guardians in the Presbyterian Church of Scotland. John Knox had led the Scottish Reformation from 1560, and the Church of Scotland resembled the kind of church many English Puritans wanted. In his 1599 book Basilikon Doron, James had written harshly about Puritans, but his comments were mainly directed at the more extreme elements, and many Puritans hoped that he might still agree to moderate reforms. In 1603, Puritan ministers organised a petition to the new king. This petition became known as the Millenary Petition, because it was signed by about 1,000 Puritan ministers. The Petition was careful not to attack the king’s royal supremacy in the Church of England, but it called for various reforms to remove ceremonies seen as popish. It complained about the use of the sign of the cross in baptism, which Puritans regarded as superstitious; it questioned the rite of confirmation, since it is not found explicitly in the Bible; it opposed the practice of baptism by midwives, which Puritans thought reflected a superstitious fear that unbaptised infants could not go to heaven; it objected to the exchanging of rings during marriage, again as unscriptural and superstitious; it criticised the ceremonial bowing at the Name of Jesus in worship; it attacked the requirement that clergy wear the surplice because it was not mentioned in Scripture; and it questioned the custom of clergy living in the church building. The Petition also argued that each parish should have a preaching minister, rather than one who only read services from the Book of Common Prayer. Against Archbishop John Whitgift’s policy that clergy must subscribe to the Book of Common Prayer and use the prescribed vestments, the Petition claimed that ministers should be required to subscribe only to the Thirty-Nine Articles and to the royal supremacy. Finally, it called for the end of episcopacy and the introduction of a Presbyterian system of church government. The Petition was presented to James at Leicester so that he would not be influenced beforehand by the bishops. James, who enjoyed theology and theological debate, agreed to hold a conference at Hampton Court Palace where supporters and critics of the Petition could present their views. After being delayed by an outbreak of the plague, the Hampton Court Conference met in January 1604. The king chose four Puritan representatives: John Rainolds, president of Corpus Christi College, Oxford; Laurence Chaderton, master of Emmanuel College, Cambridge; Thomas Sparke; and John Knewstubs. Archbishop Whitgift led the opposing side, made up of eight bishops, including his protégé Richard Bancroft, Bishop of London, seven deans, and two other clergymen. On 14 January James met only with Whitgift’s party. On 16 January he met with the Puritans. That day ended badly for the Puritans when Rainolds mentioned their proposal to set up presbyteries in England. James saw this as an attempt to weaken his authority in the church and famously declared, “No bishop, no king!” He then ended the session early. On 18 January he first met Whitgift’s group and a number of ecclesiastical lawyers, and then summoned the Puritans to hear his decisions. James ruled that the Book of Common Prayer would remain in use and that there would be no general provision for a preaching ministry. However, he agreed to some limited changes: references to baptism by midwives were to be removed; the word “absolution”, which Puritans associated with the Catholic sacrament of penance, was to be replaced by the phrase “remission of sins”; the term “confirmation” was to be replaced by “laying on of hands” to distance it from Catholic sacramental theology; and a few other minor changes were accepted. James also agreed to support the Puritan proposal for a new authorised English translation of the Bible, which led to the translation and publication of the Authorized King James Version in 1611. After the death of John Whitgift, James chose Richard Bancroft as Archbishop of Canterbury. Bancroft had argued against the Puritans at Hampton Court, and his appointment signalled that no major reforms would follow. Soon after, Bancroft presented a new book of canons to the Convocation of the English Clergy. These canons received royal approval and so became part of the Church of England’s canon law. However, the Parliament of England, which had passed the Act of Uniformity approving the Book of Common Prayer in 1559, claimed that Parliament, not Convocation, had power to make new canon law. Puritans argued that the bishops were trying to increase their own power at Parliament’s expense. In the end, James gave way to Parliament and withdrew the canons. The 1604 Parliament marks the first time that Puritans clearly allied themselves with Parliament against the bishops, a pattern that would become increasingly important in English politics and later in the English Civil War. After the discovery of the Gunpowder Plot in 1605, anti-Catholic feeling became especially intense. Since Puritans were often the most outspoken opponents of Catholics, they gained some influence in this climate. Even so, Bancroft continued to block their main reform proposals. When Archbishop Bancroft died in 1610, James appointed George Abbot as his successor. James was at this time reintroducing bishops into the Church of Scotland, though with less power than bishops elsewhere, functioning mainly as permanent chairmen of presbyteries. In 1608 Abbot had impressed James when he went to Scotland with George Home, 1st Earl of Dunbar as part of efforts to bring the English and Scottish churches closer together, and James had made him Bishop of Lichfield in 1609. His promotion to Archbishop of Canterbury was intended to support James’s project of church unity between England and Scotland. All Archbishops of Canterbury since Matthew Parker had been broadly Calvinist, but Abbot is often seen as “the Calvinist Archbishop” or “the Puritan Archbishop.” He came closer than any other Archbishop of Canterbury to openly supporting Puritan reforms. The main point on which he differed from most Puritans was episcopacy: Abbot was a strong defender of apostolic succession and the authority of bishops in the Church of England. In 1611 the King James, or Authorized, Version of the English Bible, begun in 1604, was published. It was officially an Anglican project, but many Puritan scholars helped with the work. It was first printed by Robert Barker, the King’s Printer. It was the third English translation approved by Church authorities, following the Great Bible of King Henry VIII’s reign (1535) and the Bishops’ Bible from Queen Elizabeth I’s reign (1568). At the Hampton Court Conference in January 1604, the idea of a new translation had been raised in response to Puritan criticism of existing translations; many Puritans preferred the Geneva Bible. Over time, the King James Version gradually replaced the Geneva Bible among Puritans. The King James Bible became famous for its “majesty of style” and is often described as one of the most important books in English culture and a major influence on the English-speaking world. In England it had long been common for Sunday mornings to be used for Christian worship, followed by sports and games in the afternoon. Puritans strongly objected to Sunday sports, believing that playing games on the Sabbath broke the Fourth Commandment. Their Sabbatarian views became stricter than those of most other European Reformed churches. In the early 17th century, Puritans gained influence in several localities and managed to ban Sunday sports. In 1617, in Lancashire, there was a sharp conflict between Puritans and local gentry (many of whom were Catholic recusants) over this issue. In response, Thomas Morton, Bishop of Chester, asked King James to issue a ruling. James replied with the Book of Sports, a royal declaration stating that some Sunday sports were lawful and others were not. Criticising the “puritans and precise people,” it allowed activities such as archery, dancing, “leaping, vaulting, or any other such harmless recreation,” but forbade bear-baiting, bull-baiting, theatrical “interludes,” and bowling. The king ordered all Anglican clergy to read the declaration to their congregations, but Archbishop Abbot refused to support this and directed his clergy not to read the Book of Sports. In 1618, King James put forward the Five Articles of Perth, which required the Scottish church to adopt several English practices. The Articles required kneeling at Communion, allowed private baptism, allowed reservation of the sacrament for the sick, reserved the rite of confirmation to a bishop, and required the Church of Scotland, which had abolished all holy days, to observe certain holy days again. The General Assembly of the Church of Scotland eventually accepted the Five Articles, but a large minority of Scottish Presbyterians opposed them. To English Puritans, these measures looked like a move in the wrong direction, towards more ceremonial worship and away from simplicity. In 1620 a group of Puritan separatists, later known as the Pilgrims, crossed the Atlantic on the Mayflower and established Plymouth Colony. They were led by governor William Bradford and church elder William Brewster. These Pilgrims had originally belonged to the Puritan separatist movement in England and had faced religious pressure and persecution in the village of Scrooby, near East Retford in Nottinghamshire. In 1607, Archbishop Tobias Matthew raided their homes and imprisoned some members of the congregation. As a result, the congregation left England in 1609 and moved to the Netherlands, first to Amsterdam and then to Leiden. In Leiden they enjoyed freedom of worship, but Dutch society was unfamiliar to them and they feared losing their English identity. They therefore planned to establish a colony in America. Their first settlement in Plymouth Colony was at New Plymouth, a site previously surveyed and named by Captain John Smith. New Plymouth became the capital of the colony and eventually developed into the town of Plymouth, Massachusetts. At its height, Plymouth Colony included most of what is now southeastern Massachusetts. It was one of the earliest successful English settlements in North America, alongside Jamestown and other Virginia settlements, and the first substantial permanent English settlement in New England. The colony concluded a treaty with Chief Massasoit, which greatly helped its survival. The Pilgrims also received important help from Squanto, a member of the Patuxet tribe, who acted as interpreter and guide. In 1691 Plymouth Colony was merged with the Puritan Massachusetts Bay Colony (founded in 1628 under John Winthrop) and other territories to form the Province of Massachusetts Bay. King James liked to think of himself as a peacemaker in Europe, and royal propaganda presented him as a new Solomon. In his view, the Church of England offered a model “middle way” that could be acceptable to both Protestants and Catholics. James believed that the Church of England represented a via media or middle way between Protestantism and Catholicism. When his son Charles was old enough to marry, James considered wedding him to a Catholic princess. The Thirty Years' War began in 1618, and many English Protestants demanded that James take military action on behalf of his Protestant son-in-law, Frederick V, Elector Palatine. James at first refused, but by 1620 he needed money for an expedition to help Frederick and so summoned Parliament for the first time since the 1614 Addled Parliament. Led by Edward Coke, Parliament refused to grant adequate funds unless James promised that Charles would marry a Protestant. James insisted that Parliament had no right to interfere with royal prerogative. Parliament answered with a formal protest affirming its ancient rights. Under the influence of his favourite, George Villiers, 1st Duke of Buckingham, and the Spanish ambassador Diego Sarmiento de Acuña, 1st Count of Gondomar, James ordered this protest removed from the record and dissolved Parliament. Buckingham became highly influential with both James and Prince Charles. In 1623 he persuaded the 23-year-old prince that England should ally with Spain and that Charles should marry a Spanish princess. Buckingham and Charles then travelled in disguise to Spain so that Charles could court Maria Anna of Spain, daughter of Philip III of Spain. This proposed marriage, known as the Spanish Match, was deeply unpopular with English Protestants and lent credibility to Puritan suspicions that there was a plot to bring England back to Catholicism. When James called another Parliament in 1623, the anti-Catholic feeling was so strong that it was clear Parliament would not support his policy. In Spain, the authorities insisted that the marriage would only go ahead if Charles agreed to convert to Catholicism and to spend a year in Spain receiving Catholic instruction. Under these conditions, Charles broke off the negotiations in 1624. His return to England was greeted with public celebrations and treated almost as a national holiday. After this failure, Charles favoured an alliance with France and war against Spain. At the largely Puritan 1624 Parliament, members impeached Lionel Cranfield, 1st Earl of Middlesex, the minister most closely linked with support for the Spanish Match. The Parliament then agreed in principle to fund a war against Spain, although it did not actually provide the money needed. James remained a doctrinal Calvinist all his life. When the Quinquarticular Controversy broke out in the Dutch Republic after the death of Jacobus Arminius in 1609, he supported the Calvinist Gomarists against the Arminian Remonstrants. He personally chose the British delegates to the Synod of Dort in 1618 and agreed with its strongly Calvinist decisions. However, as Puritans increasingly opposed his policies (over the Book of Sports, the Five Articles of Perth, the Spanish Match, and other issues), James began to look for churchmen who would support his more inclusive, ecumenical plans. Since Elizabeth’s reign there had been theologians in England who disliked the strict predestinarian views of high Calvinism associated with Theodore Beza and adopted by many Puritans. For example, Peter Baro, Lady Margaret's Professor of Divinity at the University of Cambridge, had resisted Archbishop Whitgift’s attempt to impose the Calvinistic Lambeth Articles on the Church of England in 1595. Some of Baro’s students at Cambridge, including Lancelot Andrewes, John Overall, and Samuel Harsnett, criticised rigid predestination in ways similar to Arminius. When James wanted allies against the Puritans, these theologians were willing, and although few of them were fully Arminian, Puritans soon began to label them the “Arminian party.” In 1624, the Cambridge scholar Richard Montagu received royal permission to publish A New Gagg for an Old Goose. Written as a reply to a Catholic attack on the Church of England, Montagu’s book argued that the strict Calvinist positions under attack were held only by a small Puritan minority and that most clergy in the Church of England rejected high Calvinism. A New Gagg was a turning point in the history of Puritanism, because it was the first time Puritans were clearly identified with a particular set of doctrinal views (and not only with certain practices). George Carleton, Bishop of Chichester and a former English delegate to the Synod of Dort, was shocked to find that his own theological position was now being described as “Puritan.” By the time James died in 1625, Puritanism had established itself in England as a powerful religious and political movement. Puritans influenced many English institutions and had spread to Holland and the American colonies, especially Plymouth Colony. They had also gained significant strength in Parliament. Under King Charles I the Puritan movement would become even more prominent and, for a time, would take control of the country through the English Commonwealth and the Protectorate of Oliver Cromwell after the English Civil War. But it was under James (1603–1625) that Puritanism gained major momentum. Many Puritan ministers and theologians during the reign of King James helped shape and expand the movement in England. Among the most important figures were Thomas Cartwright (1535–1603), a preacher, scholar, and controversialist who is often seen as the patriarch of Presbyterian Puritanism and is remembered for his disputations, letters, and his short commentary on Paul’s Letter to the Colossians; Laurence Chaderton (1536–1640), the first Master of Emmanuel College, Cambridge, a translator of the King James Bible, who lived over a century and was widely regarded as a patriarch of Puritanism; and William Perkins (1558–1602), Master of Emmanuel College, one of the most prolific Puritan theologians and biblical expositors of the Elizabethan era, known especially for his “Golden Chain of Theology” and his commentary on Galatians, whose influence on later Puritanism was immense. Other important figures included Richard Rogers (1550–1618), fellow of Emmanuel College, noted for strong biblical preaching and for his “Seven Treatises” on the Christian life; John Knewstub (1544–1624), preacher and scholar, a Puritan representative at the Hampton Court Conference and a Presbyterian-leaning but moderate Puritan; and Arthur Hildersham (1563–1632), a key promoter of the Millenary Petition and a noted nonconformist preacher. The Scottish scholar Andrew Melville (1545–1622), a leading Reformed theologian and church reformer after John Knox, also played a role in shaping the wider Reformed world and attracted many continental scholars to study at Glasgow and St Andrews. John Dod (1549–1645) was a noted nonconformist preacher and biblical expositor, famous for his “Exposition of the Ten Commandments,” which earned him the nickname “Decalogue Dod.” George Abbot (1562–1633), Archbishop of Canterbury from 1611 to 1633 and a translator of the King James Bible, acted as a partial protector of Puritan interests inside the Church of England. John Rogers (1570–1636), sometimes called “Roaring John Rogers,” was known for his fiery sermons. John Rainolds (1549–1607) was a leading Puritan scholar of the King James era, the most prominent Puritan at the Hampton Court Conference, and a major contributor to the King James Bible. Paul Baynes (1573–1616), a friend of William Perkins, was famed for his powerful preaching and his exposition of Ephesians. Stephen Egerton (1555–1621) was one of the ministers chosen to present the Millenary Petition to King James in 1603. Henry Ainsworth (1571–1622), one of the period’s greatest Old Testament scholars and an avowed Congregationalist, is remembered for his “Annotations on the Pentateuch.” Henry Airay (1560–1616), a moderate Puritan, was known for his preaching and his commentary on Philippians. Robert Parker (1564–1614), a separatist Puritan praised by Cotton Mather as one of the greatest scholars and theologians of his time, left England for Holland because of persecution. Nicholas Byfield (1579–1622) was a leading Puritan preacher and an important promoter of strict Sabbath observance, best known for his commentary on Colossians. William Pemble (1591–1623), a scholar and theologian and reader at Magdalene College, helped form Puritan thinking in the universities. John Robinson (1575–1625), pastor of the Pilgrims before their departure on the Mayflower, became an early leader of English Separatism and is often regarded, along with Robert Browne, as one of the founders of Congregationalist church government. John Preston (1587–1628), who succeeded Laurence Chaderton as Master of Emmanuel College, was considered one of the most Christ-centred preachers of his time and wrote influential devotional works such as “The Breastplate of Faith and Love.” Robert Bolton (1572–1631) was a noted preacher and scholar, author of pastoral and devotional writings including “Directions for a Comfortable Walk with God.” William Ames (1576–1633), a strict Puritan and student of William Perkins, became one of the era’s greatest theologians through his work “The Marrow of Sacred Divinity.” A convinced Congregationalist, he migrated to Holland because of persecution and became connected with the Pilgrims. Richard Sibbes (1577–1633), a moderate Puritan who remained within the Church of England, was famous for his warm, devotional preaching and biblical exposition; his book “The Bruised Reed” became a classic of Puritan spirituality. Thomas Taylor (1576–1633) was a powerful preacher and leader in the movement, known especially for his exposition of Titus. Samuel Ward (1577–1648), Master of Emmanuel College and student of Perkins, served as a delegate of the Church of England to the Synod of Dort. Richard Bernard (1568–1641), a moderate Puritan, wrote an influential handbook for ministers entitled “The Faithful Shepherd” and a popular allegory, “The Isle of Man,” which greatly influenced John Bunyan and his Pilgrim’s Progress. Henry Jacob (1563–1624), a separatist Puritan associated with the Brownists and Congregationalism, became a friend and associate of John Robinson. John Downame (1572–1652), a London preacher and theologian who later worked closely with the Westminster Assembly, is remembered for works like “A Sum of Sacred Divinity” and “A Guide to Godliness.” John Davenant (1572–1641), a respected Anglican scholar and moderate Calvinist, became bishop of Salisbury in 1621 and also served as an English delegate to the Synod of Dort. Though not always counted as a Puritan, his learning and conciliatory spirit influenced Puritan thought. He is especially known for his commentary on Colossians and for his “Dissertation on the Death of Christ,” in which he argued that Christ’s atonement was sufficient for all and effective for the elect: “Christ died sufficiently for all men, and effectually for His elect.” John White (1575–1648), a preacher and scholar chosen for the Westminster Assembly, helped obtain charters for the New England Company and the Massachusetts Bay Company and so played a key role in Puritan colonising ventures that led to the Massachusetts Bay Colony. Daniel Rogers (1573–1652), a student of William Perkins, became known for his practical and devotional preaching and his book “Matrimonial Honor.” William Gouge (1575–1653), a prominent preacher and theologian and member of the Westminster Assembly, wrote many works including “Domestical Duties” and a large commentary on Hebrews. Richard Stock (1569–1626), one of the Puritan founders of the Feoffees for Impropriations, served as pastor and tutor to the future poet John Milton. Thomas Gataker (1574–1654), scholar and theologian, was also a member of the Westminster Assembly and a close associate of Richard Stock.

Hitoshi Motoshima was a Japanese politician. He served four terms as mayor of Nagasaki from 1979 to 1995. He has publicly made controversial statements about the responsibility of Japan and its then-reigning Emperor for World War II. He survived an assassination attempt in 1990. On October 31, 2014, Motoshima died at the age of 92 in Nagasaki, Japan from natural causes.

Hitler Nababan (born 1964) is an Indonesian politician from the Democratic Party. He was a member of the Karawang Regional People's Representative Council (the city's legislative body) from 2014 until 2019. He was born in 1964, moved to Karawang in 1994. Before he was a member of parliament, he worked as a moneylender.

Hitoshi Ashida (芦田 均, Ashida Hitoshi, 15 November 1887 – 20 June 1959) was a Japanese politician. He was a leader in postwar politics. Ashida was Prime Minister of Japan in 1948. He quit his leadership responsibilities after a corruption scandal (Shōwa Denkō Jiken) involving two of his cabinet ministers.

Hitoshi Kikawada is a Japanese Liberal Democratic politician. He has been a member of the House of Representatives since 2012. From 2022 to 2023, he was chairman of the foreign affairs committee. In October 2025, he was named Minister of State for Okinawa and Northern Territories Affairs by Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi.

Hjalmar Horace Greeley Schacht (22 January 1877 in Tingleff – 3 June 1970 in München) was a German politician and minister for economics during the time of the Third Reich. In the Weimar Republic he was the president of the Reichsbank. He was also one of the 24 defendants at the Nuremberg Trials. His middle names come from the American politician Horace Greeley.

Karl Hjalmar Branting (23 November 1860 – 24 February 1925) was a Swedish politician. He was the leader of the Swedish Social Democratic Party (1907–1925), and Prime Minister during three separate periods (1920, 1921–1923, and 1924–1925). When Branting came to power in 1920, he was the first Social Democratic Prime Minister of Sweden. When he took office for a second term after the general election of 1921, he became the first socialist politician in Europe to do so following elections with universal suffrage. He won the Nobel Peace Prize in 1921 with Christian Lous Lange. He was also minister of Finance and Foreign Affairs. Branting was born on November 23, 1860 in Stockholm, Sweden. He studied at the University of Uppsala. He was married to Anna Branting. Branting died on February 24, 1925 in Stockholm, Sweden from unknown causes, aged 64.

Knut Hjalmar Leonard Hammarskjöld, born 4 February 1862, dead 12 October 1953, was a Swedish politician, scholar, cabinet minister and Member of Parliament from 1923 to 1938 (first chamber). He served as the Prime Minister of Sweden from 1914 to 1917. In 1890, he married Agnes Almquist (1866–1940). The couple had four sons: Bo, Åke, Sten and Dag.

Ho Jong-suk (; July 16, 1908 – June 5, 1991) was a Korean politician, journalist and independence activist. One of her main topics of interest was feminism. Her courtesy name was Jongja(정자, 貞子) and her pen name was Sukayi(수가이, 秀嘉伊). Historical rememories of great loves (위대한 사랑의 력사를 되새기며)

Hlengiwe Buhle Mkhize MP (6 September 1952 – 16 September 2021) was a South African politician. She was a member of the National Assembly from 2009 until her death. She was Minister of Home Affairs in 2017 and Minister of Higher Education, Science and Technology from 2017 until 2018. Mkhize died on 16 September 2021 at the age of 69.

Hocine Aït Ahmed (; (August 20, 1926 – December 23, 2015) was an Algerian politician. He was founder and leader of the historical political opposition, Socialist Forces Front, in Algeria until 2009. He was born in Ain El Hammam, Algeria. Arrested and sentenced to death in 1964, he escaped from the El Harrach prison on May 1, 1966. Exiled in Switzerland, he became a doctor of law. Aït Ahmed died at age 89 in Lausanne, Switzerland on December 23, 2015.

Hojatollah Khatib (; 1954 – 26 April 2015) was an Iranian sports administrator. He was the chairman of multisport club Persepolis Athletic and Cultural Club based in Tehran between July 2004 and December 2005. He was also a wrestling president. He died from cancer in Tehran, aged 61.

Hollis Loyd Harris (November 25, 1931 – July 14, 2016) was an American businessman. He served as President and COO of Delta Air Lines (1987-1990) and Chairman, President, and CEO of Continental Airlines (1990-1991), Air Canada (1992-1996), and World Airways (1999-2004). In 1997, Harris and Steve Wolf signed a strategic agreement between Air Canada and United Airlines, producing what is now the Star Alliance, which grew to become the world's largest global airline alliance. Harris died at the age of 84 on July 14, 2016 in Peachtree City, Georgia.

Holger Mathew Pihl, Jr. (September 23, 1928 – October 3, 2018) was an American Republican politician and judge. He was the Circuit Court Judge of Washington County, Oregon until 1995, and then a Senior Judge until his retirement in 2005. He was appointed to the court by Oregon Governor Tom McCall in 1976. Pihl was born in Portland, Oregon. He studied at the University of Oregon and at Northwestern University. Pihl died on October 3, 2018 in Manning, Oregon at the age of 90.
Holly J. Mitchell (born September 7, 1964) is an American politician. She has been a member of the Los Angeles County Board of Supervisors since 2020 as a member of the Democratic Party.

Holly Black née Riggenbach (born 1971) is an American writer and editor for Children's and Young Adult Fiction. She has won many prizes. She is a New York Times bestselling writer. Holly Black's work has been changed by people into more than 30 languages. She has wrote over 30 fantasy young adult books so far in her work. Some of her young adult books are The Cruel Prince and The Prisoners throne. She has 48 total prizes for her books. She has written with other people 42 books so far. Black holds B.A. in English from The College of New Jersey. 2006: Andre Norton Award for Young Adult Science Fiction and Fantasy, Valiant: A Modern Tale of Faerie 2014: Mythopoeic Fantasy Award in Children's Literature, Doll Bones 2014: Newbery Medal Honor Book, Doll Bones 2015: Indies Choice Book Award—Young Adult Book of the Year, The Darkest Part of the Forest

Holly McKeever Cairns (born 4 November 1989) is an Irish politician. She has been the leader of the Social Democrats party since March 2023. She has been a Teachta Dála (TD) for Cork South-West since 2020. She was a member of Cork County Council for the Bantry local electoral area from 2019 to 2020. Cairns was born in Cork and worked on her family farm which made organic seeds. She volunteered in many charity organisations in Malta and Romania before starting her political career in Ireland. She became active in politics because she supported LGBT rights and abortion rights. She joined the Social Democrats in 2018. Cairns ran in the 2020 general election as a candidate in the Cork South West constituency. During her time in the Dáil Éireann, she focused on the agricultural businesses of Cork. As a TD, Cairns is known for criticizing the government of Taoiseach Micheál Martin. She did not support the government's response to the Commission of Investigation Records about Mother and Baby Homes not releasing personal data to victims. In March 2023, Cairns became leader of Social Democrats, replacing Róisín Shortall and Catherine Murphy. During her time as leader, she has shown support for Palestine while criticizing the Irish government and European Union for their support of Israel. She has also refused to merge the Social Democrats with the Labour Party. Cairns supports solutions to fight climate change and homelessness in Ireland. Cairns led the party through the 2024 general election, in which the party gained seats in the Dáil Éireann. Holly McKeever Cairns was born on a farm in Cork, Ireland. She studied in organic horticulture from University College Cork. Her mother, Madeline McKeever, was a Green Party politician. Cairns worked on the family farm, Brown Envelope Seeds, making organic seeds. During the 2010s, Cairns lived outside of Ireland, spending some time working in an orphanage in Romania, before moving to Malta for four years. In Malta, Cairns worked for a charity organisation called INSPIRE which gives educational services to children and adults with disabilities. Cairns first entered politics as an activist interested in LGBT rights and abortion rights. Cairn joined the Social Democrats in 2018. She was one of the founding members of the West Cork branch of the party. Cairns was elected to Cork County Council for the Bantry local electoral area in 2019, winning the last seat by a single vote. During the campaign, she was against the creation of a plastics factory in Skibbereen. During her time as a councillor, she created the Inside the Chamber podcast about local government. In 2019, she proposed a motion for councillors to receive documents three days before voting, which was passed. She was a member of the executive committee of Carbery Housing Association until her election to the Dáil. Cairns ran in the 2020 general election as a TD candidate in the Cork South West constituency. She was the youngest Social Democrats candidate, being 30 years old. She ran against her then-boyfriend, Christopher O'Sullivan of the Fianna Fáil party. She was elected, taking the third and final seat, winning 4,696 (10.59%) of the vote. Cairns was the only female TD elected in all of Cork City and county. She then became the Social Democrat Spokesperson for Agriculture, Food and the Marine; Further and Higher Education; and Disability. In March 2020, Cairns was criticized by farmers for her "lack of support" for the dairy business in Cork. That same month, she supported the creation of a task force to support the fishing business. In October 2020, Cairns criticised the Commission of Investigation (Mother and Baby Homes and certain related Matters) Records for not giving access to survivors of the institutions to their personal data. Cairns was also worried about the sealing of the archive in the Dáil. She did not support government's role in not taking any of the amendments from the oppositions. After the Dáil voted in favour of the legislation, she said that she was "sick to my stomach that the State has let the survivors down yet again... The amount of emails, phone calls, and letters I have had on the Mother and Baby Homes Records is overwhelming. People want justice and accountability for the survivors of these horrific institutions." After the bill was passed, Taoiseach Micheál Martin promised Cairns that survivors would be able to get access to their records. In November 2020, Cairns was against a parliamentary motion to give state funding to the greyhound racing industry. Wayne McCarthy, a board member of Greyhound Racing Ireland, called her an "ignorant little girl" on Twitter. McCarthy's comments were called sexist and offensive by many politicians. Speaking in the Dáil, Cairns said that she did not want to use her Dáil speaking time to talk about, what she called "everyday sexism", but that it cannot be ignored. She invited McCarthy to a public debate about funding the greyhound racing industry. Despite this, in 2021 the government gave €19.2 million in taxpayer money to funding greyhound racing. In April 2021, Cairns asked the government to spend more money for national treatment for eating disorders after a constituent went to Cairns asking for help. In May 2021, she questioned Taoiseach Micheál Martin, after he publicly supported an appeal against the construction of a €140 million cheese factory in County Kilkenny. Cairns said that the factory would be a way for the Dutch to keep making money from dairy products while cutting their herd numbers to meet environmental standards. Cairns also said that Martin had told Cairns it was not right for government members to be part in planning issues when she talked about the idea of creating a mother and baby home in County Cork. Cairns announced on 26 February 2023, that she would run for leader of Social Democrats. No one else ran in the leadership election, so Cairns became the new leader. She took over leadership of the party on 1 March 2023. After taking office, Cairns said that the Social Democrats have no plans in merging with the Labour Party. The first poll taken after she was elected leader showed that the party's support had more than doubled to 9%. Cairns is a supporter for an "Irish NHS" to fix the problems of the current healthcare system in Ireland. She supports action to fight climate change, calling it a threat that cannot be ignored. Cairns has called housing in Ireland a "national crisis" and supports policies to fix the housing shortage. Cairns has also talked about against false information about asylum seekers and believes in showing support for them instead. As leader of the Social Democrats, Cairns has showed support for Palestine. She also said that Israel has done war crimes against Palestine and called on Western leaders for a ceasefire. After Israeli invaded the Gaza Strip in 2023, the Social Democrats called for the removal of the Israeli ambassador to Ireland, with Cairns saying the European Union's response to the war in Gaza as "despicable". In November 2024, Cairns led the party into the 2024 general election, in which the party won five seats more seats in the Dáil Éireann while winning 4.8% of the vote. She was the only woman elected in any Cork constituency at that election. In late June 2025, Cairns said that she would not run for president in that year's presidential election. Cairns was in a relationship with Cork TD Christopher O'Sullivan of Fianna Fáil but the couple ended their relationship in 2020. In January 2023, Cairns said that for six months the year before, she was harassed by an online stalker. The stalker eventually showing up at her home in West Cork many times. She said this after many Irish women in politics such as Jennifer Carroll MacNeill said that they had been harassed for being women. In June 2024, Cairns announced that she and her partner, Barry Looney, were expecting a baby girl. She said that she was happy since she had two miscarriages the year before. Cairns became the first Irish party leader to have been pregnant in the Dail. She announced that the Social Democrats' deputy leader, Cian O'Callaghan, would lead the party during her maternity leave. She gave birth to a girl on 29 November 2024, the day of voting in the general election.
Homer Martin Adkins (October 15, 1890 – February 26, 1964) was an American Democratic politician who was the Governor of Arkansas between 1941 and 1945.

Homero Gómez González ( – January 2020) was a Mexican environmental activist, agricultural engineer and politician. He was the manager of El Rosario Monarch Butterfly Preserve, a part of the Monarch Butterfly Biosphere Reserve. Gómez was mayor and commissioner of, Michoacán. Gómez was last seen alive on 13 January 2020 attending a meeting in the village of. More than two weeks after his disappearance, his body was found in an agricultural reservoir in Ocampo, aged 50.

Hong Joon-pyo (born 20 November 1953), also spelled as Hong Joon-pyo, is a South Korean politician. He was the presidential nominee of the Liberty Korea Party in the 2017 South Korean presidential election. He unsuccessfully ran for president again in 2025. Hong is often seen similar to U.S. President Donald Trump and has been nicknamed "Hong Trump" due to his campaigning style. He was the Chairperson of the Liberty Korea Party from July 2017 to June 2018.

Cielito "Honeylet" Salvador Avanceña (born February 17, 1970) is a Filipina businesswoman. She is best known for being the current partner of former Philippine President Rodrigo Duterte. Avanceña and Duterte have been in a relationship since at least 1996 and have a daughter named Veronica. Shortly after the inauguration of his husband as president, Avanceña was not named as First Lady. Her step-daughter Sara was proposed to fulfill the role instead who did not accept the offer. Avanceña would carry out the roles usually done by the First Lady.

Hong Gi (Hangul: 홍기, Hanja: 洪基) (3 March 1916 – 20 July 2004) was the wife of South Korean President Choi Kyu-hah. She was the first lady when Choi Kyu-hah was in office, from 1979 to 1980. Hong Gi was born in 1916 in Chūshū, Chūseihoku-dō (today Chungju, North Chungcheong Province, South Korea), the eldest of three daughters of Hong Byung-soon and Kwon Jae-hee. Her grandfather was a known Chinese scholar, and she learned Chinese from a grown-up. As a result, she did not attend a regular educational institution. In 1935, she married Choi Kyu-hah, who was three years younger than her. Between 1935 and 1943, Choi went to study at higher institutions in Japan and Manchukuo. During this time, she lived with her in-laws. In 1964, Choi was appointed as South Korean Ambassador to Malaysia. As a result, she went with her husband to Kuala Lumpur where they lived together. During this time, she learned English while serving as the wife of the ambassador to Malaysia, and happily served as the hostess as the ambassador's wife at the garden reception. On 1967, Choi was appointed as Foreign Minister. On 1975, Choi was elected as the Prime Minister of South Korea. During this time, Hong took care of the kitchen and laundry herself. Hong's role may change a lot depending on the change of Choi's position, but she has always stayed in the shadows. When Choi Kyu-hah became the acting President of South Korea after the assassination of Park Chung-hee in 1979, Hong became the First Lady of South Korea on December 6, 1979. Her tenure as First Lady is the shortest in South Korean history. During her time at the Blue House, Hong only took the lead in supporting nursing homes and orphanages, but refrained from outside activities. Secretaries who have been with her for 20 to 30 years remember her as an adult who is fair, respects principles, and has contributed greatly to helping her husband to be honest. On the other hand, she is evaluated by those around her as having a strong character that is as strong as a man. She was forced to step down from her position as First Lady in August 1980, after Major General Chun Doo-hwan and close allies within the military staged a coup d'état against Choi's government in December 1979. After stepping down as president, Choi and his family lived quietly out of the public eye. Hong Gi suffered from Alzheimer's disease in her later years. As a result, Choi took care of his wife, while at the same time looked after his ailing health also. Choi would often visit Seoul National University Hospital, where she was admitted to. She was the friend of Lee Hee-ho, wife of former South Korean President Kim Dae-jung. On July 20, 2004, Hong Gi died of Alzheimers at the age of 88. Her remains were initially buried at the Seoul National Cemetery. When her husband died two years later, her remains were relocated and reinterred at a special tomb site alongside Choi in the Daejeon National Cemetery.==Personal life== Hong and Choi Kyu-hah have three children: sons (Choi Yun-hong, Choi Jong-seok) and daughter (Choi Jong-hye). Honorary Recipient of the Grand Order of Mugunghwa (1979)

Hong Sa-ik (hangul: 홍사익, hanja: 洪思翊, born February 2, 1887 – September 26, 1946) was a military general for Japan, but he was from Korea. In September 1905, Hong Sa-ik entered the Korean empire military school but switched to a Japanese military school in Tokyo after Japan took over the country. He joined the Japanese military. From 1910 until 1936, he served in the army and he was promoted to general. In 1940, he was appointed to work in the city of Nanjing in China. In 1944 he was sent to the Philippines, where he was put in charge of prisons for captured Allied soldiers. In August 1945, Japan was defeated by the American army and other Allied forces. Hong Sa-ik tried to escape, but he was arrested by the American army. He was called a Class B war criminal, meaning that he committed crimes that are not unusual in war, like harming the prisoners in his camps. But the Allies did not think he planned the war or committed crimes against humanity, like the Nazis who ran the Holocaust. On September 26, 1946, he was executed by firing squad with other Japanese generals.

Hong Nam-ki (; born 29 July 1960) is a South Korean politician. He was the Minister of Economy and Finance and Deputy Prime Minister of South Korea under President Moon Jae-in from November 2018 to May 2022. In April 2021, Hong became the Acting Prime Minister following the resignation of Chung Sye-kyun.

The Hongwu Emperor (October 21, 1328– June 24, 1398), known in China as Zhu Yuanzhang, was the first emperor of the Ming part of China's history. The Hongwu Emperor's real name was Zhū Chóngbā. It is written [[:wikt:en:朱 in Chinese writing. His given name was Chongba and his family were the Zhus, but Chinese people write their family names first. His name means "Double Eight", which is a lucky number in Chinese culture. People say his parents called him that because their ages at the time added together to make 88. He was also their eighth child. In old China, there were many rules about names and who could use them. People used boys' real names but, when they became men at age 20, only older members of their families could call them that. Other people used a special courtesy name to be polite. When he became a man, Zhu Chongba chose the name Xīngzōng, meaning that he wanted to bring success in honor of his dead family members. This name is written [[:en:wikt:興 in the traditional writing used on Taiwan and Hong Kong and [[:en:wikt:兴 in the simplified writing now used by the PRC. When he started to become a successful leader, he started to use a third name: Zhū Yuánzhāng. This name is written [[:wikt:en:朱 in Chinese writing. He also sometimes used the courtesy name Guóruì, meaning "National Luckiness". In old China, the Chinese emperors did not number their years from one place. Instead, they gave names to eras (groups of years) any time they wanted. Some emperors made 10 or more eras while they led China. Zhu Yuanzhang started his era when he took Khanbaliq (now Beijing) from the Yuan emperor Toghon Temür in 1368. He said this was the 1st year of the "Very Warlike Era", which sounds like Hóngwǔ and is written [[:wikt:en:洪武 in Chinese. He only had this one era when he was emperor, so people also called him the "Emperor of the Hongwu Era" or Hóngwǔdì ([[:wikt:en:洪武). When he was the emperor of China, Chinese people just called him the "Emperor". If they met him, they used very polite terms like Bìxià ([[:wikt:en:陛下, "Your Highness") to speak to him. After he died, the next emperors gave him a new, long, and very polite name and called him Míng Tàizǔ ([[:wikt:en:明), the "Greatest Dead Family Member" of the Ming. After the Xinhai and Communist changes in government of China, people are less polite when they talk about the old emperors. They usually just call him by his everyday name Zhu Yuanzhang like a common person. In English, it's more common to talk about him as the Hongwu Emperor. Zhu Chongba was born on October 21, 1328, during the Yuan part of China's history. His father ZhuWusi ([[:wikt:en:朱) or ZhuShizhen ([[:wikt:en:朱) and his mother Chen Erniang were farmers near a small town called Zhongli near the Huai River in central China. Today, it's within Fengyang, Anhui. His family had so little money that they had no land themselves and needed to borrow other people's farmland. They could not feed all their children and had to give away some of them to other people. When Zhu was 16 years old, there was no rain for a long time. Because only a little food could grow, everyone left in his family died except for Zhu and one of his brothers. Not knowing what else to do, he joined the Huangjue Buddhist temple as a monk. It did not have much money either and could not give him food for very long, so he soon left. He walked around, asking people for money or food, for about 3 years. Then he went back to Huangjue Temple and stayed there until he was 24. The other monks at the temple taught him to read and write. People were very angry with the Yuan leaders of China at the time. They were Mongolian people, but most Chinese were Han. Many people started fighting the government. The Yuan army would stop them but hurt many people as they did. Then more people joined in fighting the government. Zhu was one of these. An army destroyed his temple and he started joining the people fighting against them in 1352. He quickly became a leader and joined his fighters with the Red Turbans. In 1356, he took Nanjing and made it the capital of his own small country. He made laws and kept his people mosty safe, so many more people left to join him. This made him even stronger. In 1368, he took Khanbaliq (today's Beijing) and started the Ming Empire in place of the Yuan. He died on June 24, 1398, and was followed as emperor by his grandson Zhu Yunwen, who became the Jianwen Emperor.

Honoré III, Prince of Monaco (Honoré Camille Léonor; 10 November 1720 – 21 March 1795) was a reigning prince of the small state of Monaco. He succeeded his mother Louise Hippolyte and is to this day still one of the longest reigning European rulers. The eldest surviving son of Princess Louise Hippolyte of Monaco and her husband Prince Jacques In May 1732 he moved to Paris to be with his father till he was officially proclaimed the prince of Monaco. Antoine Grimaldi, the Chevalier de Grimaldi, acted as regent for the prince between 1732 and 1784, when Honoré chose to live in Paris. This situation remained the same for half a century until Antoine's death in 1784, On 5 June 1757 he married Maria Caterina Brignole a member of one of the most powerful and wealthy familys in the Republic of Genoa. The had two sons before divorcing in 1770. Prince Honoré IV of Monaco (17 May 1758 – 16 February 1819) married Louise d'Aumont and had children. Prince Joseph of Monaco (10 September 1763 – 28 June 1816) married Marie Thérèse de Choiseul and had children. 20 February 1731 - 17 May 1758 His Serene Highness The Marquis of Baux. 7 November 1733 – 19 January 1793 His Serene Highness The Prince of Monaco, Duke of Valentinois.

Honorius (Latin: Flavius Honorius, c. 384 - 15 August 423) Was a Western Roman emperor from 23 January 393 until his death on 15 August 423. Honorius inherited the Western half of the Roman Empire after the death of emperor Theodosius I, while his brother Arcadius inherited the Eastern half. His reign was pretty chaotic with constant civil wars and revolts and in 410 AD, Rome was sacked for the first time in 800 years by the Visigoths.

Hope Pym is a fictional superheroine from the Marvel Comics universe. The character was created by Tom DeFalco and Ron Frenz, and first appeared in A-Next #7 (April 1999). She is the daughter of superheroes Hank Pym and Janet van Dyne in the MC2 universe. Hope Pym is a supervillain known under the codename Red Queen. Evangeline Lilly portrays a different version of the character, Hope van Dyne, in the Marvel Cinematic Universe movie Ant-Man (2015) and appears as the successor of the Wasp in the movies Ant-Man and the Wasp (2018), Avengers: Endgame (2019), and Ant-Man and the Wasp: Quantumania (2023). Lilly returned in the animated series What If...? (2021) as an alternate version.

Horace Greeley (February 3, 1811 – November 29, 1872) was an American newspaper editor, reformer, and politician. His New York Tribune was the most influential newspaper from 1840 to 1870. Greeley used it to promote the Whig and the Republican Parties. He is best known for his socially-colored journalism. He wanted to convince people of his ideas such as his opposition to the expansion of slavery. He thought that the role of a journalist was to convince people with sound arguments. He did not like the sensationalist approach of Joseph Pulitzer and others. Greeley ran for president and was nominated by the Democratic Party in 1872 but died before the election results came. However, he would have lost to the Republican candidate, Ulysses S. Grant.

Horace Mann (1796-1859) was an educator and politician who helped set up the first public schools in the United States. He did this in the state of Massachusetts. Mann personally visited every school in the state to inspect it. He later became the first president of Antioch College in Ohio. “Our means of education,” he stated, “are the grand machinery by which the ‘raw material’ of human nature can be worked up into inventors and discoverers, into skilled artisans and scientific farmers.”

Horacio Manuel Cartes Jara (born 5 July 1956) is an Paraguayan politician. He served as President of Paraguay from 2013 through 2018. Cartes won the 2013 presidential election in Paraguay on 21 April 2013 and took office as President on 15 August 2013. Horacio Cartes is the owner of "Grupo Cartes", a conglomerate of approximately two dozen of companies. He has also been president of the football club Club Libertad since 2001

Horace G. Burrell JP OM (8 February 1950 – 6 June 2017), also known as Captain Burrell, was the president of the Jamaica Football Federation, and a Vice-President of CONCACAF.
